utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. The Chamber is not aware of any preliminaries. Therefore, we'll patiently wait until the witness is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Boering.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday. Mr. Stojanovic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I hope you're ready to answer a few more questions, and those questions will be about the third meeting, as we call it, or the meeting that was held in the morning on the 12th of July in Fontana Hotel. Do you remember whether on that occasion your delegation had received any instructions from the Ministry of Defence of the Netherlands with regard to the treatment of the population in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we did not receive any additional directions other than what I already indicated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up a video-clip, 65 ter 28780. It is V0009266. I'm interested in the portion of that video that starts at 13 minutes and ends at 14.17 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, sir, this video-clip is actually the ending of that meeting. Colonel Karremans says that he did receive an order from the Ministry of Defence. He says, and I quote: "I received the instruction this morning to assist as much as I can." What should have been that assistance? What would it have consisted of, the assistance that Colonel Karremans is referring to?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that assistance concerned caring for the refugees as much as possible as well as our own DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you returned to Potocari, before you set out towards Tuzla and Kladanj with the first convoy, did you have an occasion to see the activities of UNPROFOR members while the civilian population was being loaded onto the buses?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw some activities, I walked around, and I also returned from Potocari to Bratunac to check some details. Yes, I had the freedom to drive and walk around.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that UNPROFOR members together with Serbian troops protected the population with their own bodies and let them go through to the buses?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether there was any protection by UNPROFOR of the refugees to enable them to board the buses, the agreement was that first the wounded and the children would leave on the buses and that one DutchBat military man would accompany each bus because of time pressure imposed mainly by the VRS. This didn't happen. The buses were filled as quickly as possible and drove off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we continue I'd like to verify one of the previous answers. Mr. Boering, one of your answers was recorded - and it's the second half of your answer - as: "Yes, I had the freedom to drive and walk around." Is that what you said in your own language or did you say something like: "I had some freedom to drive and walk around"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say I had some freedom to drive and walk around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you observe the activities of UNPROFOR members on that day during the population evacuation process?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that and, among other things, I asked them actively to observe several matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you see that the population was willingly boarding the buses, that due to the situation and the dire straits in which they were in they wanted to board the buses as soon as possible? Did you observe that as well?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I observed was that it was very hot at that point and a large group of people had not had anything to eat or drink for quite a while - they were in a hopeless situation - and the buses were a way of being able to depart. So a group of people wanted to leave by bus, hoping to be taken to a better place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice the vehicles that had brought in bread to the population that was there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me when I say that at that moment the Dutch Battalion did not have any reserves of food, that they could not possibly feed the population that was there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had limited supplies and we certainly could not care for that large group for several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you also agree with me that the number of population, including women, children, and elderly, constituted a humanitarian risk due to the conditions that surrounded them should they have stayed there any day longer?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you also agree with me that given the number of the population that was there, nobody in the local commune was in a position to provide enough food and medical care as well as any other assistance for a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And given your position and your contacts, do you know who it was who told the local population that there was a decision for them to leave their homes and set out towards Potocari, if indeed there was such a decision in the first place? So if there was such a decision, whose decision it was and who communicated that decision to the population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's take it one by one. Was there such a decision that the local population should leave their homes and set out towards Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have to speculate, then you don't need to answer my following question. However, given your position, given your experience, and bearing in mind the configuration of the enclave, could that have been a spontaneous decision or, alternatively, should there have been a plan in place for the population to start moving?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are asking for a judgement rather than anything else, Mr. Stojanovic. Therefore, if you would put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I appreciate the comment, and now, Your Honours, with your leave I would like to call up the debriefing 65 ter 19416. As far as we are concerned, it doesn't have to be broadcast. I'm interested in page 30, 3-0, in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is this a document where you consider it better that it not be brought to our screens? Is that what you are referring to? So then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- if you would then give me a moment -- yes. And what is now on our screen will not be -- yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that I would like to see your answer on page 31. I will read it as well. In that conversation that you had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is this a debriefing document related to this witness? Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I suppose that you have read the last paragraph on this page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we then go to the following page, where you will find your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which document am I supposed to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you have that page in English in front of you. I'm interested in the last paragraph in italics. It is a question that was put to you, and then on the following page you will find your answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if we do not show it for the public, you're invited to read slowly the text you are referring to so that everyone is able to follow the question without perhaps all the names specifically being put on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked: "You hadn't in that brief moment ... had you talked about it with one another? How do we interpret what is going on here? Or was there just no time for that? The point is whether you, too, were already looking for explanations, which were given later, as it was already very quickly clear to some people, according to their statements, that there was something fishy going on there. For a number of people it takes perhaps a full day before they get it, 'something's not right here' ..." I'm asking you this, sir: Did you discuss that with your colleagues immediately on the spot, as it were? Did you have an occasion to do that? And your answer was this, you mention names, and you say: "As I've already said, I went there. What's going on here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether the page we have is what you're reading. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the following page, you have the answer now, the first paragraph on page 31 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've got page 32 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 31, please. This is the page, paragraph 1, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "As I said," you mention a certain name, "I went there quickly. What's happening here? I quickly stationed the UNMOs. I just told," and you mention another name, "what the situation was and then quickly left. That some of our people were there with tape and were engaged in allowing groups through and possibly also helping with the selection. 'Men go over there. You need to be in that house.' "Q. Had you all had the opportunity? It was not unknown that your people helped to carry out selection. "A. Yes, that's a sensitive subject. "Q. I realise that this involves your colleagues," says the interviewer, "but just ..." And your answer is this: "It's a sensitive subject. You know. So sensitive, in fact, that one colleague was detained," and then you mention the name of the institution "for nearly a year ... that's a well-known fact, I think. After a bit of assistance that was rendered in terms of singling out. That made him number one on the list. It's sensitive. You know." I would like to ask you is this: You provided this statement to a certain body over a decade ago. Does this jog your memory to the fact that you saw UNPROFOR members with tape allowing groups of civilian population to go through towards the buses?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the interpretation perhaps was not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I mentioned the tape - and I was referring to your answer - could you please explain the Trial Chamber what you actually saw. What did you mean when you said "the tape"?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I remember is that UNMOs were busy at a building watching where men were being taken away who were selected. I remember that about the UNMOs. And I had asked them to watch the number of the Muslim men who were taken in so that they knew the numbers afterwards. As for being busy with tape, I remember that there was tape, but whether those UNMOs or our soldiers, I thought that those were our soldiers trying to regulate the flow of refugees more so. The group with large numbers was divided into groups contained with a white tape. That's what I remember about the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let me finish with this question: Did you notice that some of the UNPROFOR members were assisting with the selection, saying men should go this way, you have to go into that house?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. I only asked them to be at that house to watch what was happening. So I assigned them or I asked them to watch what was happening, but I wasn't in command of them, I didn't have that authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that according to military regulations it is fully legitimate when you have POWs to make a selection, conduct a triage, and to check whether such a group of people contains persons who might be suspected of having committed war crimes?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that seems like a standard procedure if you're -- that you interrogate POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the fact about those checks which, as you say, General Mladic also mentioned contains nothing that would be disputed or questionable from a military point of view; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- Mr. Stojanovic, could we make a clear distinction between facts and legal analysis. I'd like to have a few matters clarified. The portion you read to Mr. Boering was -- and part of the answer of Mr. Boering was about UNMOs. Now, in your next question you said: "Let me finish with this question: Did you notice that some of the UNPROFOR members were assisting with the selection ..." Now, did you want to start a new topic, not about UNMOs any further but about UNPROFOR, or was it that you wanted to give a follow-up to the previous question and the previous answer which were about UNMOs? Could you clearly explain what you -- what your question was in relation to the previous questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The question had to do with UNPROFOR members and I finished that with the question about military observers. It was one military observer, you had the occasion to hear him; and now I'm asking this gentleman about the engagement of UNPROFOR members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it was -- you moved away again from UNMOs and you returned to UNPROFOR members. Then for the next one you asked questions about selection and triage of prisoners of war. I think it's important to make a clear distinction between facts and law. So the first, I think, appropriate question to Mr. Boering would be whether he considered the men present there to be prisoners of war and on what factual basis he thought they were or on what factual basis he thought they were not, and then we can ask -- you can ask your further questions. Mr. Boering, the men around, did you consider them to be prisoners of war? And I'm more interested in the factual basis on which you would rely, if forming an opinion about that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw several of the men in that white house, where they were already locked up in the first stage. And as I saw them, at that point they were certainly not fighters; they were refugees who were trying to leave with the flow of refugees from the enclave if that happened. I did not have the impression that these were fighters. A combatant can be made a POW, but these were not soldiers in my view. So I do not see them as POW status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I asked you before is to -- less about your judgement on the matter but more about the facts on which you rely. So if you say: I saw them, I did not consider them to be combatants or fighters or -- therefore, they should not have been taken prisoner of war, I would like to know what facts you observed which may have been relevant for forming your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not armed. I saw that the VRS soldiers were removing men from among the refugees and taking them to that building. There was certainly no military action by the people who were being taken away, so I do not regard them as soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said they didn't carry any arms --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- did they carry anything at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the clothes that they were wearing and that was all, ordinary civilian clothes. They were not wearing military attire nor were they recognisable as pertaining to any military group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber has seen pictures before showing luggage. Did you see any of those men carrying any luggage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes refugees had some light luggage. What you could take with you, you were carrying. And generally they would contain clothes, food, and beverages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could it be expected that someone who was a soldier would throw away his weapon and decide to join the civilians and in this way leave the area where combat was going in a situation when there were so many people?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could be some among them, but, for example, the spokesman of the refugees who I had found the -- on the night before and I know for certain that he was not a military person who didn't want to carry a weapon. So my response is: Yes, there could have been some among them but that I didn't observe that. It didn't strike me as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. And did you know that a man whom you knew as someone whom you identified as a possible negotiator was a soldier and had been wounded and that that was a reason why he was no longer militarily engaged?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that nor did I see that he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that at one point UNPROFOR members began to compile a list of able-bodied men and, indeed, made such a list of people they had registered?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that they were working on a list of names, but I thought that that list related more to the wounded but I was not involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know on whose orders this registration or compilation of a list was made.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could have been Colonel Karremans or Major Franken. They were working on a list and I think that that list concerned the wounded in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that at one point able-bodied men were prohibited from entering the UNPROFOR facility?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was said that we don't want any military or men between age 16 and 60 in the facilities - I do remember that generally - or wounded or women and children who needed assistance, because the camp where we were there was relatively little space.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your answer during the debriefing which you have in front of you, you say the following when asked whether it was true that your men helped with selection: That this is a sensitive topic and that one of our colleagues was even taken into custody because of this. Do you remember that? Do you remember this fact? And does it refresh your memory with regard to the activities of UNPROFOR on that day?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this may sound strange, but I simply can't remember that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that you have the text of your answer in front of you. It says - let me not mention any names: "It's a sensitive subject. So sensitive, in fact, that one colleague was detained," and then it's mentioned who detained him, "for nearly a year. That's well-known, I think." Is that something you don't remember today?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to insist on that any further. I will just ask you to look at another short video-clip --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, yesterday you indicated that you needed another 15 minutes today. Well, you're now 45 minutes on your way. Mr. Shin announced that he would need most likely 15 minutes. I wonder whether we would be able to finish during this session because you took half an hour more, three times the time you indicated you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding, Your Honour. If I may ask just one additional question, one area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that at one point while you were in Srebrenica, together with Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans you received the invitation to attend a celebration organised by the authorities of the enclave on which occasion a video-clip was played showing the Muslims taking a few Serbs from a tank and cutting off their ears. Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that we were invited to an activity because that video was played in the middle of that event. In any case, somebody was removed from a tank and was beaten and that was -- it was clearly indicated at the meeting that that was sufficient that we didn't appreciate that and didn't want to see it and certainly didn't appreciate it and wanted to have no part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that as a provocation on part of the enclave authorities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Provoking who, Mr. Stojanovic. My question was: Provoking who? A provocation against who? I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel and you, sir. That is Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans. If they invite you to a celebration and then show you such a video for which they say that it includes examples of instances at which Serbs had their ears cut off, this is what you said. You said that they played that to you for dessert.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was at the end of a dinner, a celebration. But once again, I did not see ears being cut off because at a certain point we said: That's enough. We don't want to see any more. And I think we left fairly soon after that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you allow me I would finish with this question and I would just tender into evidence to be MFI'd because of translation 65 ter 19416 which I used during my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin -- Mr. Mladic, would you please remain seated. Mr. Shin, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you remind us what it was, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I proposed that the document 65 ter 19416 be admitted into evidence and that it be MFI'd at the moment because of translation issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the debriefing of the witness? Is that, Mr. Stojanovic -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is in the -- in the Dutch version it's 77 pages. I think in the English version it is 50 pages or something like that. I think it's a good habit in this courtroom that a party seeks to tender those portions they dealt with during the examination of the witness and that the other party can ask for context to add to that in order to better understand the selection. Do you want to make further selection or do you want to tender the whole of it? And is there any specific reason then to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I would then tender into evidence specific pages that I referred to from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that you make a selection, announce in court which selection you have made, and perhaps already give notice to Mr. Shin so that Mr. Shin can consider whether he wants to add for context other portions as well, and that we then decide on it. I see that you agree --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with that procedure. Mr. Shin, we have five minutes left to the moment where we usually take a break. You announced 15 minutes yesterday. Does that still stand?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I expect actually to use somewhat less than 15 minutes, but rather than break up the re-direct if it's suitable to take a break now, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break now. Now, I hope that the fact that we first take a break, just as we yesterday adjourned, will not lead to taking three times the time as announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I can certainly undertake that will not happen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will not happen. We'll take a break and we will resume at a quarter to 11.00, but only after the witness has left the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 10.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Perhaps meanwhile, Mr. Stojanovic, does the objection against admission of P1139 marked for identification still stand, that is the transcript of the previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, considering the suggestion. And if I may use this opportunity, we also identified the pages and we are sending our list to the Prosecution to see if we can agree on the pages that we would like to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Shin would have a look at it, and then may I take it that it will be admitted in three languages: Original, English, and B/C/S? Then we'll wait for -- meanwhile, Madam Registrar, if I'm not mistaken the 92 ter transcript in this case was assigned number P1139? And the associated exhibits to which Mr. Stojanovic already -- said already that there was no objection against admission, that was P1140 up to and including P1146. Therefore, P1139 up to and including P1146 are admitted into evidence. At the same time, Mr. Shin, I have to repeat what I said earlier that admission of this transcript now does not mean that the Chamber will not use its discretion in the future if not as an exception but -- I wouldn't say as a rule but too frequently transcripts are sought to be admitted under Rule 92 ter. Let that be a clear message. Then, Mr. Shin, if you're ready to re-examine Mr. Boering, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, Your Honours. And the Prosecution did take the opportunity at the break to reduce the amount of time anticipated for re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Boering. During cross-examination yesterday, counsel -- Defence counsel played a segment of a video of the first Fontana meeting, and that was 65 ter 28780 from 43 minutes, 8 seconds, to 45 minutes and 15 seconds. I would like to play now -- and let me just say that that portion related to Colonel Karremans describing a request from UN BH command regarding withdrawing from the enclave. I'd like to play the next 38 seconds following that very clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could please begin with 45 minutes and 15 seconds and play until 45 minutes and 53 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: "Karremans: There are some woman who are able to speak English. And what I've heard from all those other soldiers who are now working to -- let's say to ease the pain for the population, a lot of people, a lot of persons, women, said: We are waiting for the buses. Can we leave the enclave? "Because they are sick, they are tired, they are very scared."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be this -- perhaps the same audio problem. Could we re-play it and have the volume for Mr. Mladic a bit higher up. And, Mr. Lukic, it would certainly assist if Mr. Mladic would use the usual headphones because that gives less problems, but let's have the volume turned up and let's play it again. No further comments, please. Let's play it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Karremans: There are some women who are able to speak English. And what I've heard from all those soldiers who are now working to -- let's say to ease the pain for the population, a lot of people, a lot of persons, women, said: We are waiting for the buses. Can we leave the enclave? Because they are sick, they are tired, they are very scared."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Boering, my question to you: Now we've just heard Colonel Karremans talk about the pain of the population and speak of women who are asking to leave the enclave: "Because they are sick, they are tired, they are very scared." To your knowledge, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's accurate. The situation was generally without any prospects, and after several days of poorly eating and drinking and little sleep, this group was basically exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. The questions in re-examination have not triggered any further need to further examine the witness, Mr. Stojanovic, as I see, which means --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means, Mr. Boering, that this concludes your testimony before this Chamber. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to this court and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we ask the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, the Chamber would like to deliver a short oral decision on a procedural matter. The Chamber will deliver its decision on two Defence motions requesting extensions of time to respond to Prosecution Rule 92 bis motions. In the first motion filed on the 9th of April, 2013, the Defence requests an additional 150 and 180 days respectively to respond to the Prosecution's 22nd and 23rd Rule 92 bis motions, which were filed on the 26th and the 27th of March, 2013. The Defence further requests clarification of the legal effect of the Chamber's guidance with respect to Rule 92 bis motions, submitting that the Prosecution's concurrent filings of such motions is in contravention of the Chamber's guidance. Finally, the Defence submits that the Chamber has neglected to give specific dates for past dead-lines for responses to Rule 92 bis motions and that oral rulings on requests for extensions have not clearly specified what was granted, preventing the Defence from adequately addressing all filings. In the second motion, filed on the 16th of April of this year, the Defence requests an additional 90 days to respond to the Prosecution's 24th and 25th Rule 92 bis motions, both filed on the 3rd of April. The Chamber recalls that its guidance pertaining to the filing of Rule 92 bis motions specified that such motions should be filed at least two to three weeks apart in order to give the other party sufficient time to respond. This can be found on transcript page 108. On the 28th of September of last year, the Prosecution made an oral submission requesting an increased filing pace for certain Rule 92 bis motions, with a view to completing such filings by the end of February 2013. This is at transcript page 3311 and was further discussed in court at transcript pages 3896 to 3899. The Prosecution expressed its standing position that it would not object to any application by the Defence seeking additional time to respond to these motions, if its request were to be granted. On the 12th of October, 2012, the Chamber granted the Prosecution's request, thereby amending its original guidance, but making clear that it would entertain Defence requests for extensions of time with a view to ensuring adequate response time. This is at transcript page 4057. As such, the Defence submission that the Prosecution has violated the Chamber's guidance is misguided and the Chamber sees no need to revisit its current practice. It notes, further, that since the amendment of the original guidance, the Defence has filed several motions requesting extensions of time to respond to incoming 92 bis motions, all of which were granted, most of them fully and some in part. Further, while the Chamber considers that all dead-lines for pending Rule 92 bis motions have been clearly communicated to the parties, either by e-mail and put on the record shortly thereafter or by oral ruling directly in court, as it is apparent that the Defence requires clarification in this regard, the Chamber will again put these dead-lines for future responses due on the record. It will do it in chronological order. The Chamber granted the Defence request for an additional 60 days to respond to the Prosecution's 16th Rule 92 bis motion, setting the response date to 29 April 2013. By granting an additional 66 days to respond to the Prosecution's 18th Rule 92 bis motion, the dead-line was set to the 13th of May, 2013. Finally, on the 8th of April, 2013, the Chamber put on the record its decision to extend the dead-lines for responses to the Prosecution's 20th and 21st Rule 92 bis motions with an additional 60 days, thereby fully granting the Defence request and setting the response date to these motions to the 27th of May, 2013, which can be found at transcript page 9521. Turning to the Defence requests for additional time to respond to the Prosecution's 22nd and 23rd Rule 92 bis motions, the Chamber is not inclined to grant the requested 150 and 180 days of extension respectively, as it considered this a disproportionate amount of time. Considering that the last Rule 92 bis related dead-line for the Defence is currently the 27th of May, 2013, the Chamber hereby decides that the Defence dead-line to respond to the Prosecution's 22nd Rule 92 bis motion will be two weeks from that date, namely, the 10th of June, 2013; and for the 23rd Rule 92 bis motion, the dead-line for a response hereby becomes the 24th of June, 2013. Lastly, concerning the Defence requests for an extension of time to respond to the Prosecution's 24th and 25th Rule 92 bis motions, the Chamber grants the requested 90 days' extension in full, thereby setting the dead-line for responses to these motions to the 16th of July, 2013. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. Can the next Prosecution witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be excused, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we could save a little time if we handed out this next exhibit to the Chamber. I know the Defence already have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are invited to do so, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you. Good morning, Ms. Gallagher. This is the follow-up on your examination-in-chief, so therefore it was only recently that you were reminded that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. That still is the case. And I don't think we have to establish your identity because that's been done already as well. Mr. McCloskey, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning. As you know, we've asked you to come today to talk about the -- what we all refer now as the trial video which is 65 ter 28780 and what we refer to as the stills book 65 ter 28781. And I think you may have seen the Judges were just passed out the stills book. First of all, can you briefly describe -- and bearing in mind that, as you know, you've seen brief clips of the trial video played to the Court already so they have some knowledge of it, but can you tell us what is this trial video and what role did you play in its creation?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a compilation of many different video-clips about actually 25 different source videos that have been compiled into one trial video, and it's really meant to document the events of Srebrenica as they were happening at that time. So predominantly they focus its footage that focuses from July 10th to about July 20th, 21st, but there is also some other videos that are related to Srebrenica that are incorporated into this trial video a little bit before and little bit after the Srebrenica events. My role has been both adding some portions of videos, at times being a part of the process, sitting with the director or the editor, choosing which clips to put in. I have also been a part of creating the stills book which accompanies the video and have been a part of also interviewing some of the people that are identified in the book and in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go through some questions as we do. Do you know roughly how long this trial video is in its compilation?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's over four and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you distinguish the material in the video from, say, the material Mr. Ruez did pursuant to the investigation? Is the material in this trial video specific to the particular time-frame?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's meant to capture the events as they were happening at the time. So it's not a later re-visit or a documentary going back to Srebrenica in recent years; it is capturing the footage that existed by TV, by those people that were on the ground videotaping it, of those events mainly in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll go over just a section in the table of contents of a book to get an idea of that, but -- now when you said the editing, can you tell us, is this an edited product? Is there any material where the process did not edit out material but put in the entire grouping of things we had? Can you tell the Court a little bit about the editing or lack thereof as went into this four and a half hour video?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course it is an edited trial video. There's a lot more footage that exists out there than could possibly have gone into the video. So there -- and there's a lot of repetitive or duplicative videos out there that the ICTY has received so we're not going to put any duplication in. The idea was to capture the most complete and best-quality footage that existed, and sometimes, yes, there's footage that has to be edited out because it -- it's too long, it's not relevant to -- let's say to the case. Sometimes we or the film-maker has used different clips to try and get the complete footage. Maybe one clip is not complete and another clip is complete, but the incomplete clip is better quality so a combination of the two would be used to have the most complete and best-quality clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say a "film-maker," who are you referring to and what was that job?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was somebody that was hired in 2002 to come in and actually make this video, Marta Fracassetti came at the time and was the one that put together this trial -- this original trial video, not this current one that we'll be seeing today but the original one, along with the Srebrenica trial team. So together they were able to put together this trial video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we'll notice when we see the video that it will go suddenly from a certain quality of picture to another quality of picture and sometimes with even a different logo as it continues. Can you explain why that is?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's actually what I was just trying to say a moment ago, where you might have incomplete footage that's, let's say, from -- for example, from the BBC that's very good quality and then there's other complete footage, more footage, that comes from the local Srpska Radio Television network as an example. And we want to make sure that the entire interview or the entire story is captured. So I know, for example, Marta had used the incomplete and then added the complete footage which was not as good a quality. And you'll see sometimes where it switches back and forth but it's just to make it the most complete and full clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, now let's go to 65 ter 28781, the -- what we call the stills book which the Court has in front of them and we can see it's entitled: "Trial video Srebrenica." But let's go to page 3 in e-court which is basically the first page of a table of contents. And can you just explain to us how this begins to show us how the trial video and the stills book is organised? Can you just explain this briefly to us so we can understand the organisation a bit better?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both the trial video and the stills book lays out the footage chronologically so that the book parallels the trial video, and the trial video is split up into chapters. And you'll see there's 38 chapters. And it notes the different clips that were used in each chapter. So you'll see the source, where the video -- original video footage came from, when the ICTY acquired it, and then a little bit about the footage itself that's in the trial video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you take part in producing this table of contents?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've put most of it together but it's also been the work of other people. It originated when Marta made the first original video, so that was the core of it. And I've added to it. We had a criminal analyst who also had worked on the video and one of our attorneys also has played a substantial role in putting this together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's the basic purpose of the stills book?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just -- it's to highlight some of the parts of the video that we want to point out. There are key individuals that are in the trial video that we've captured stills of. So we wanted to highlight those and how -- who they are and how they were identified as well as locations. So it's just to help guide the video as you're watching the video to know who the people are, where they are, what is the context of what you're seeing on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Is it meant to ideally be flipped through as one watches the video to help identify who some of these folks are?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you play a role in any of those identifications?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have. I have identified a number of the people that are in the trial video, and you'll see when I have identified them it's noted in the stills book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it is -- it's not our intention or my intention today to go through each of those identifications certainly, but can you give us an example of how you would have identified some of the people from the video? For example, Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was one of the defendants in the Popovic trial so I spent a few years seeing him in court and seeing that he testified and he identified himself in the trial video and of course know who he was through the course of the investigation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any other examples of how you would have been able to identify folks besides the accused in the -- well, I won't call them accused but the people in the former trials?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also from -- well, I've interviewed a number of the people that are in the video and identified them from my own personal interviews with them or speaking with others who had identified them, looking -- yeah, it's mainly been through my own personal identification or sometimes it may be other -- through other sources, open sources, or other people who have assisted me in identifying who the person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would that -- when you say "other people" assisting you, could it be a person -- well, a Muslim witness? A VRS person? Or a MUP person that you've interviewed that would have identified someone in the video? Would that also be included as part of the sources for this identification?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are also some of the other sources of the identification other investigators from the OTP that have made the identifications?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And you'll see those noted also in the book when it's been another investigator that made the identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where in the book does it note the source of the identification?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once you get past the table of contents you'll see the book is made up of individual photographs with a description under each photograph, and it's there you'll see who has made the identification and by what means or how and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we'll also see in the book that there's -- should be four DVDs attached in the back in little -- what are those four DVDs?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the DVDs that make up the trial video. They didn't all fit onto one CD or DVD so they're broken up into four. And you'll see that the table of contents reflects what's on each DVD.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's begin to go through some of the book to give the Trial Chamber and everyone an idea of what this is about, and then we'll - with leave of the Court - actually play some of the trial video. So let's go to page 13 in e-court in the book which is page 1 in the book itself. Now, we see here that this is just the title of this particular chapter and we see 10 or 11. How do you explain the "10 or 11 July 1995"?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The footage we received -- well, it didn't say which date it was. We can -- we can assume from the context that it was either the 10th or the 11th of July as the VRS were approaching were Srebrenica. Sometimes we can't tell if it's, you know, footage from the afternoon of the 10th or the morning of the 11th. So just out of cautiousness and not wanting to overstep our certainty, we have let you know that it's one of these two days and we're not a hundred per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we also see here "Antelope" and then "WTN - Reuters" and "SRT." Can you tell us -- I think we've all heard of Reuters but can you tell us what these other things are basically?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right this is a -- this page is a chapter break and this is the first chapter. So each chapter will look like this. It's the title of the chapter, the date, and then the footage, the source footage that we got the videos from and that are incorporated in this chapter. So, for example, Antelope is a production company that made a film called: "A cry from the grave." And they had source material that we obtained from them. WTN, World Television Network, and Reuters is more of a news agency clearing house that buys and sells news footage. And then the SRT footage is the Srpska Radio Television footage, the local television journalists that were also out in the field at the time in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As far as you know, did the Srebrenica investigation know precisely where Antelope productions got this footage?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They gave the OTP a list of the source materials that they had used in making "A cry from the grave." So we have seen what they used and so, yes, we do know the footage that they used. Sometimes we might not know -- always know the details. It might say it's a Muslim civilian they got it from and we might not know the name. They won't -- have not described the name of the Muslim civilian, but basically we know how and where they got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page of the stills book. It's page 4 in e-court. Page 14, I'm sorry. If we could blow that up a bit. All right. And is this where the video starts here?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see here that it's been identified as a Zvornik Brigade Praga and with a registration number vehicle log Zvornik Brigade with this conclusion that it belonged to the Zvornik Brigade. Can you tell us where this information was gathered? On this still we really can't make out much in the way of licence plates or registration of the -- of this first machine coming at us.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: On our own video equipment we're able to blow it up and see it much more clearly so it's -- there's no doubt the registration number is 11067. We were able, and the team prior to my arrival, was able to obtain vehicle logs from the Zvornik Brigade during a search and seizure in 1998, and of these original vehicle logs there is a log for a Praga as part of the Zvornik Brigade with that registration number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you point out to us where the number is on this particular still, the registration number, if you can make it out just so we know - I don't think we can read it very well - but so they know where this is coming from?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you're looking at the front it's just above the left tire, so to the left side of the little bike that's hanging there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, "left" meaning from viewing it from this which would normally be considered to be the right front tire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Let's look at just one more example like this on the next page, 15. We see here a tank also registration number 6717, again from the Zvornik Brigade. How did we sort this out?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same way as the prior Praga. It's from the Zvornik Brigade search and seizure of original documents. There was a vehicle log that had this tank with this registration number, the 6717, noted on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on this photo can you actually see the registration number?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you see it better above the tank, gunner aimer's head there on the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, Mr. President, I -- the suggestion now would be to play some portions of this trial video that we've chosen and occasionally I might ask or anyone could ask Ms. Gallagher about that, but this is important video that we would like the Court and the world to see. We have picked out potentially up to one hour and five minutes of video for your viewing, most of which -- in fact, the vast majority of which you have not yet seen. I do not intend to play Hotel Fontana and other parts of the trial video that you have already seen. And so in that event we would start the playing of it with a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, when you're saying one hour and five minutes, which would mean that with questions it would take far more time, thus not just looking at it continuously? What portions do you have in mind to play? Five minutes or ten minutes or two minutes before you stop and either ask questions or ... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There won't be very many questions and we have divided up the times and given brief titles of the segments we intend to play on the sheet that we hope all have received and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we have received ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The latest update is in our e-mail. Let me just check whether I have got it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I can assist you by just briefly going over it as you requested. The first segment which is about five -- four and a half, five minutes is the shots of the VRS approaching the Srebrenica along the road. You can see the stills. And that will include some news footage from the RS of the similar things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have -- I have on my screen at this moment a list which is dated -- it's one page. It gives a list of parts of 28780 and I find a date at the right bottom side, 19th of April, 2013, and apart from the list it also has a short chapter prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and I can just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just wanted to verify whether we have in front of us what you refer to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Mr. McCloskey suggests that we look at those portions. Have you considered -- I mean, do we have to play it twice if you want to put questions or would that be a possibility -- Mr. McCloskey, I'm looking at you as well, that if Mr. Ivetic would have a specific question whether he could ask for it to be stopped so that we avoid that we have to go through it twice. Mr. Ivetic, is that something that would be agreeable to you or would you suggest another way of proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, at least with the prior witnesses that have dealt with this video that we have always played it once and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- in cross-examination we'll refer to the actual time in the transcript when they were talking about a particular video segment. I don't know whether we've actually played anything repeatedly in cross, but that's not my intention to repeat any video in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine if there are specific questions about a specific portion that we would have to look at it again and that you select the portions so that we don't have to play the whole of the video again. Then, in the absence of any objections, we'll proceed as you suggest, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I -- I have no objection if something comes up that Mr. Ivetic thinks he can deal with at -- during the direct that he interrupts, that's no problem. And of course Ms. Stewart would also on cross take us all back to exactly where Mr. Ivetic wants to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you can see as she has done with Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Ivetic nodding, yes. He agrees apparently. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's -- I think this particular chapter's fairly self-explanatory so let's just play it where we identify on the sheet, 00.29.0.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would just add that you can try to keep up with the book if possible because it's designed ideally to go along with it, but not critical I don't think at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Stopping at 1.50.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The man with the red hair, the book identifies it, was that one of the people you were able to identify?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We just spoke of him, Vinko Pandurevic, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Here we are at 1.57.9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The book identifies the person but can you tell us who this is?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Milan Jolovic with the nickname Legenda. He is the commander of the Drina Wolves who is -- who are part of Zvornik Brigade under the Drina Corps, and he is also, as you see, on the road co-ordinating with his units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's this blurry red markings up in the top -- well, above Legenda's head?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the logo for Srpska Radio Television in it looks like -- well, CPT, it's SRT, and some of the footage we had received from the Srpska Radio Television network directly and they had been broadcasting it so you will see throughout the entire trial video this logo and you know directly that that comes from Srpska Radio Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this could be any military operation or anything. What do you believe that this is having to do with from what he's talking about and where he is?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right it's along the southern approach to Srebrenica from Zeleni Jadar. Both -- we know that from the placement of the tanks and the Pragas that were noted in the vehicle records. We know that from people that have testified, including Vinko Pandurevic, as to roughly where they are along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and this is where we designed to stop at 4.57.8. And I believe it's a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is a good time to take a break. We'll take a break and we'll first invite Ms. Gallagher to follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at five minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll continue, Ms. Gallagher. Mr. McCloskey. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now -- and we don't need this on the screen but we left off -- we're now at the chapter entitled: "Srebrenica town 10 July Muslim civilian footage," but the Chamber has seen some of that already including the Muslim mortar squad and -- so let's skip ahead from page 6 in the book to page 13 in the book and the video will -- but before we get to the video we see that in the book it's called: "Gathering of Bosnian Muslim men and boys, the location on the road from Srebrenica to Susnjar 11 July." Can you -- and that's page 25 in e-court, though we don't need to bring it up. We'll soon see the video. That's just for the record. Can you tell us the source of this video we're about to see?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This comes from a Bosnian Muslim man who was living in Srebrenica who was videotaping the gathering and leaving of men and women in Srebrenica, and I have read his -- he had given a statement to the OTP in 2002. I have read his statement where he describes the video footage he took.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do we know precisely where this is or generally?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He states in his -- in his statement that it is the exit of Srebrenica and the video footage continues as he's moving along towards Susnjari. It ends several hours later after you see the time-stamp here where he says they are near Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But the clip we've chosen for the trial video is pretty -- pretty short; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It's not the entire -- it's not the entire video-clip that he -- and not the entire footage he took.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when -- have you looked at this and seen any weapons among -- counted or made any effort to count weapons as you looked at this?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't made any effort to count weapons, but I've noticed the men, some boys, occasionally some women that are amongst the group. I believe that you see a couple weapons but most of them don't appear to be armed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's play that. It should be 14.13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't ask you to identify who that was. All right. That's a short clip ending at 15.07.4, and the next chapters in the book are parts that we've already seen of General Mladic and some of his command going down the road towards Srebrenica. So let's go to 21.09 which we call: "Mladic in Srebrenica." Now, was there any effort to try to put in all the Mladic footage of Mladic in Srebrenica as opposed to editing it out?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's correct. Everything that the OTP has regarding Mladic and Srebrenica is included in this trial video. There's nothing that has been left out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So I think we should just play it and follow along as best we can in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I see we've started there, and I now recall why. This -- and we're at 21.11.5. This person that's holding this helmet in their left hand, I think we'll recall, was this blue helmet that Mr. Ruez spoke about. And has the investigation come up with an identification of this man?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, actually. Drazen Erdemovic had identified him in the testimony in Tolimir that this was a man from the 10th Sabotage which is the same unit Drazen Erdemovic was with and his name is Cico.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have his full name or no ?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Drazen Erdemovic only mentioned his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Here we are 25.11.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can hear General Mladic calling out to Zile and Krle. Can you tell us, had those names been identified as nicknames for anyone?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zile and Milenko Zivanovic the commander of the Drina Corps at that time, and Krle is General Krstic, the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the identification was based on ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You'll actually see them appear into the screen in just a moment, but over the course of the investigation, over seeing other videos, intercepts, I've also known their names -- their nicknames through other means as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we continue on at 25.11.1, where we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you identify the smiling person on the screen now at 25.43.6?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that's Milenko Zivanovic who you heard referred to as Zile.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't spend the time to go back, but did you see Krstic a bit before that in the film?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. I know he's walking along there with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, let's just briefly go back. Sometimes these faces get too familiar for us and I forget. We're at 25.23.7. Do you see General Krstic anywhere on that film?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's the one who's the furthest to the left as we're looking at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And Drazen Erdemovic identified any of those guys in black that are standing next to him?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the two men in black, the one that had put the flag in the pile of wood there, those are two men from the 10th Sabotage that are in the unit with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they're identified in the stills book that you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then if we could continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We've stopped it at 28.54.2. And this is actually e-court page 36 but page 24 in the book to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall who this person that's shaking hands with General Mladic is?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Mirko Trivic. He's the commander of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is did he testify and help with some of the IDs of some of the people we see in this portion of the video?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He identifies himself and several of the others in the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've stopped at 30.51.9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From this video do you know who the two people are? We're at page -- it's actually page 28 in the book, 38 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the right that's still Milenko Zivanovic. To the left side that is Vujadin Popovic, chief of security for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I find that on page 26 in the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was just corrected, yes, 26. Thank you, Mr. President. All right. Let's continue there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just remind us who these -- well, we see General Mladic's back to us now and to the -- we're at 31.29.8. Can you remind us who these other three people are and describe where you see them?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the far left, that's General Krstic. In the middle with the moustache and T-shirt, once again that's Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. And the one who has his arm up in the air is Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've stopped at 32.48.8. This is page 29 in the book, 41 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But can you identify the person in the far right of the screen who's behind General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Milorad Pelemis. He is the commander of the 10th Sabotage in which Drazen Erdemovic is part of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. The chronology goes into the evening of 11 July and the Hotel Fontana which I think I will skip. And if we could go now and beginning the chapter 12 July, it's page 40 in the book, 52 in e-court, but it's noted at V0009266 from 1700 to 01.19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. McCloskey, the last portion we saw there was apparently an instruction to unscrew something and take it off. I don't know whether that's anything special. I did not have the time to really look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can certainly -- as Ms. Gallagher may have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gallagher, is there anything -- I saw that unscrew something which was on the wall --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was the sign for the Srebrenica municipal building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course what I wondered whether that is similar to the one we saw on that table in Hotel Fontana. That's -- have you further analysed that in any way or ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've wondered the same thing but I actually don't know if it's the same one or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, at least we have a picture now of what we see. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we start at that point and -- first of all, can you just -- tell us -- this is dated 12 July and what are we about to see, just basically?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very quick clip of Srebrenica on July 12th and initially you're going to see a dead body with a lot of blood coming out from it from under him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what significance, if any, is that to the investigation?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drazen Erdemovic had described being in Srebrenica on July 12th in this area next to the mosque and that a member of his unit, of the 10th Sabotage, was ordered by Milorad Pelemis who you saw on the earlier clip, to cut the throat of a Muslim man. And that person did cut his throat and Drazen Erdemovic identifies him in a proofing and in testimony in Tolimir that he believes this is the man who was killed when he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you said that Erdemovic was in Srebrenica town on 12 July; is that correct? Or is --

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, sorry. They were there on the 11th. The -- this clip is from July 12th, so it's the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's play this clip then at 17.9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We just ended at 19.3. Now let's go ahead somewhat through the chronology past the Hotel Fontana meetings and past some of the scenes in Potocari which some of -- which the Trial Chamber has seen before and go to a section. It's page 73 of the book which is 85 in e-court, and this is what we've entitled: "A Zivanovic speech at St. Peter's and Paul's patron day in Vlasenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just give us the briefest of backgrounds about what we're about to see -- not the speech itself, but where is this and what is it?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. It's a celebration of St. Peter and Paul's day in Vlasenica. It's held at a particular person's house who you see there actually in the clip standing. Zvonko Bajagic is his name. He lives in Vlasenica. And in a moment you'll see Milenko Zivanovic give a speech, a fairly lengthy speech --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again what page are we in the book, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 74, I think, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 74, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the -- -

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On the video we are at 32.29.0, and we have just watched the basics of the speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go back a little bit to this man here who just smiled briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know -- we're now at 38.41.8. Do you know what position this man held and can you tell from the video?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a bishop of Zvornik and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can -- yes, just verify it is in the stills book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we stop it for a second? Mr. McCloskey, the Chamber is puzzled by the relevance of looking at a long speech. I can imagine that there are one or two portions that we saw until now which are of some relevance about what to do with the mosque but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know hearing it like this you don't always catch everything, but sprinkled throughout it are things like the -- with the permission of the commander we set up forward command posts as we went towards the attack. And the talk about the -- destroying the minaret and the mosques --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed that that may be -- but, okay, please proceed. We wondered whether another selection could have been made but if it's still ahead then I'll take it it will come to the surface in relative -- for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we are getting to something you will recognise and it was one of these decisions where I felt like the context and some of what he's saying may be something the Defence would want me to put into context so we decided -- and I understand that it's a long -- but we just made that decision. We are very conscious of trying to make this as targeted as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Ms. Gallagher, do you know if that last reference to St. Peter's and Paul's, did that help you date this at all, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ERIN GALLAGHER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, St. Peter and Paul's day is on July 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
